proposals.relationship: Eley describes Marxist materialism as a formative starting point, acquired first through historical and political mediation before sustained reading of Marx.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:13 explicitly rejects a story of systematic early direct reading;15names1859preface as touchstone and23locates serious Marx/Engels reading in graduate school.16–17/190–191retain later critique of foundational materialism while valuing interconnectedness and scale. Engels and British Marxist mediators retain separate credit; original Marx/Engels editions unread. No simple lifelong doctrinal identity or causal determinism asserted.

proposals.relationship: Eley credits Thompson’s Making with renewing his belief in history and shaping his politically engaged historical formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:4–5 narrates Paul Slack introducing the1968Pelican discussion, then Eley obtaining Gollancz hardback and reading it during winter;13/26–29places it in British Marxist formation. Personal retrospective, not formal supervision. Later173–180 explicitly values Steedman’s gendered critique of the heroic class narrative; no unqualified adherence or original Thompson/Steedman reading by this audit.

proposals.relationship: Eley identifies Hobsbawm’s work as a major route into Marxist social history and later reclaims its ambition to connect subjects to society as a whole.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:13names Primitive Rebels/Labouring Men and jointly Hobsbawm–Rudé Captain Swing;11and25–26explicitly use1971history-of-society ambition while rejecting restoration of causal sovereignty of economy. George Rudé’s equal coauthorship retained;13calls joint study especially exciting, not sole Hobsbawm accomplishment. Originals unread; later critical recovery differs from universal agreement.

proposals.relationship: Eley identifies Raymond Williams’s cultural criticism and interdisciplinary practice as central inspirations for becoming a historian.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:19–24 explains cultural ordinariness, structures of feeling and cultural materialism and explicitly names personal inspiration beyond professional history.22–23separates later theoretical formulations from what he understood as an undergraduate;147–148retains qualifications about empire/ethnocentrism and non-Western genealogies. Raymond not Eric or Gwyn Williams; original books and exact editions not independently read.

proposals.relationship: Eley credits Genovese’s essays with perhaps his first serious encounter with Gramsci’s ideas about culture and ideology.

proposals.relationship: Eley credits Scott’s gender analysis as a necessary interpretive resource while resisting purist choices between social and cultural history.

proposals.relationship: Eley uses Catherine Hall’s histories of nation, empire and citizenship as an example of combining cultural analysis with broader social explanation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:199–201 names Hall’s work alongside Steedman and Auslander to substantiate his argument that macro questions and cultural methods need not be opposed. A particular historiographical model in his program, not sole invention, formal mentorship or endorsement of every Hall interpretation. Catherine not Stuart Hall; originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Eley develops Foucault’s account of discourse and genealogy as a way to question how archives produce historical evidence.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:128–129 explicitly reconstructs discourse, discontinuity and the archive as material event/conditions of possibility, arguing this complements rather than simply replaces empirical work. This is conceptual engagement in Eley’s argument, not automatic biographical formation or every claim about field-wide Foucault reception. n25/254says Eley uses a different translation of a passage; n26separately identifies1981method interview. Original Foucault texts/translations and every reception study unread.

proposals.relationship: Eley challenges Charles Tilly’s social-science framing for insufficiently questioning the cultural construction of ordinary people and everyday experience.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:118–122recalls the1979jointCharles/LouiseTilly conference and distinguishes organizers’ framing, Charles’s intervention and published two-callings formulation.122calls the latter unexceptionable as far as it goes but inadequate without constructed categories; this is substantive methodological criticism, not just a report of meeting behavior. Louise’s different gender/work intervention and Scott collaboration remain distinct; original conference/publishedTillysources unread.

proposals.relationship: Eley criticizes Descent into Discourse for caricaturing cultural history as political retreat, while acknowledging its careful explication and the exhaustion of older class-political optimism.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005:187–189 names Palmer’s particular book/argument and contrasts it with his own experience of the cultural turn as politically enabling. He does not deny economic/class analysis or advocate abandoning it;189–203argues against simple restoration and for pluralist societal history. Original Palmer book unread, criticism remains Eley’s attributed judgment, not total career dismissal.
